title: OffSec OSCE
summary: The Offensive Security Certified Expert, usually shortened to OSCE, was a practical, hands on certification from OffSec for penetration testers who could go beyond running existing tools. It sat at expert level, above OSCE's own entry exam, and it was widely treated as evidence that a candidate could find and exploit vulnerabilities by understanding how software actually breaks. Candidates had to complete a long, proctored lab under time pressure and then write a professional report explaining each finding, which made the exam as much about discipline and documentation as about technique. The skills it covered, including exploit development, network and web application attacks, and reporting, remain directly relevant to today's advanced penetration testing exams. OffSec retired this certification and now points candidates towards its current advanced practical exams, so treat the outline below as a study map of the skills rather than a live syllabus, and confirm the current offering with OffSec before you plan anything. This is an independent study guide and is not affiliated with or endorsed by OffSec.

beginner.definition: This was an expert level, practical certificate from OffSec for penetration testers. A penetration tester is a security professional who attacks systems with permission. The owner of those systems then fixes the weaknesses. The exam was a long hands on lab, not a set of multiple choice questions. You also had to write a report about what you did.
beginner.whyItMatters: Clients pay for results, not for tool output. This certificate proved that you could find a weakness, build your own working attack, and explain the business impact clearly. It opened doors to senior penetration testing, red team and exploit development roles. It also showed employers that you can keep working under time pressure without cutting corners.
howItWorks: Build strong foundations first, because you need programming and operating system knowledge before attacking anything.
Learn how memory is used by a running program, including the stack, the heap and how a crash is caused.
Study common vulnerability classes in depth, such as buffer overflow, format string and injection flaws.
Practise writing your own exploit code in a lab you own, and repeat each exercise until you need no notes.
Learn to pivot through a network, which means using one compromised host to reach systems behind it.
Rehearse the exam conditions, including writing a clear report while the clock is running.
beginner.example: Imagine a bank vault with a strong door. Most attackers try keys copied from other people. A skilled one studies how the lock is built instead. He notices that a spring can be pushed too far, and opens the door with a piece of wire. The bank then changes the lock design instead of blaming the wire. This course taught that deeper understanding of a system, so it took longer to learn than tool commands.
takeaways: You should be comfortable with programming and memory concepts before you begin this level of study.
Time management and clear report writing matter as much as finding the flaw.
OffSec retired this certification, so check which advanced exam is current before you plan your path.

objectives: Explain how a program uses memory and how that knowledge leads to an exploitable flaw
Develop and debug working exploit code instead of relying on ready made tools
Identify and exploit weaknesses in network services and custom applications
Perform web application attacks that reach the underlying operating system
Move through a network from an initial foothold to further systems
Document each finding with evidence, impact and a practical fix

chapters.title: Programming and exploit development foundations
objectives: Read and write code in a systems language well enough to modify a target program
Describe how a process uses memory, including the stack, the heap and the registers
Explain how an input longer than expected corrupts memory and changes program flow
Write a script that automates a repeated testing step instead of doing it by hand
Use a debugger to inspect a running program, set breakpoints and read a crash
Explain why a crash proves a flaw exists but does not by itself prove exploitation

chapters.title: Network service exploitation
objectives: Enumerate the services a target host exposes and identify the software behind each one
Match a discovered service to a known vulnerability class and test it safely
Build a reliable exploit for a vulnerable network service and explain each step
Handle common obstacles such as memory protections and limited payload space
Choose a payload that gives a usable session without breaking the service
Confirm the level of access you obtained and record the evidence

chapters.title: Web application exploitation
objectives: Map a web application, including its parameters, sessions and hidden functions
Test input handling for injection, file handling and access control weaknesses
Turn a web flaw into command execution on the host where the application runs
Bypass common filters and validation checks that try to block an attack
Explain the difference between a proof of concept and a reliable, repeatable exploit
Describe the business impact of each web flaw you demonstrate

chapters.title: Client side and privilege escalation
objectives: Explain how an attack delivered through a document or browser can start a foothold
Escalate from a low privileged account to administrative rights on a host
Identify misconfigured permissions, services and scheduled tasks that allow escalation
Move from one compromised host to other systems inside the same network
Collect and reuse credentials found on a compromised system in a controlled way
Keep a clear record of every action so that the client can follow the path you took

chapters.title: Penetration testing methodology and reporting
objectives: Plan an engagement, including scope, rules of engagement and points of contact
Manage limited exam or engagement time by prioritising the most promising targets
Write a report that states each finding, its evidence, its impact and a practical remedy
Explain a technical flaw to a reader who is not technical without losing accuracy
Store and handle client data during and after an engagement in line with the agreement
Review your own work and identify what you would do differently next time
